title: Quality & Security Gates
scopeHtml:
Scope: the test pyramid, static analysis and quality gates, DevSecOps scans, flaky tests, release gates.

Scope: contract tests, load tests, ephemeral environments, dependency updates, supply chain, code review.

notes.title: The test pyramid and what runs when
notes.html:
Different tests cost different amounts, so run many cheap ones and few expensive ones.

          /\        E2E / UI        few, slow (minutes), brittle
         /  \       Integration     some, real DB/queue (seconds-minutes)
        /____\      Unit            many, fast (milliseconds)
  • Unit: one class/function, no network. Run on every commit.
  • Integration: components together with real dependencies (Testcontainers, Postgres). Run on every PR.
  • Contract: service A's expectations of service B's API are checked (Pact) so teams can deploy independently.
  • End-to-end / smoke: a few critical user journeys against staging/production after deploy.
  • Load / performance: scheduled or before big releases.

Quality metrics: coverage (a useful floor, not a goal; 100% coverage can still miss bugs), mutation testing, flaky-test rate.

Worked example. 5,000 unit tests in 2 minutes, 300 integration tests in 8 minutes, 15 E2E tests in 10 minutes. Putting E2E on every commit makes feedback 20+ minutes; running them only after merge to staging keeps PR feedback near 10.

Industry examples. Google's testing size classes (small/medium/large); Spotify moved from heavy E2E to contract-based "honeycomb" testing for microservices.

Everyday analogy. Car factory: inspect every bolt (unit), each assembled engine (integration), and test-drive a few finished cars (E2E).

Common interview traps.

  • The "ice-cream cone": mostly manual and E2E tests, few unit tests.
  • Treating coverage percentage as proof of quality.
  • Ignoring flaky tests; each retry hides real failures.

notes.title: Static analysis, linting and code quality gates
notes.html:
Static checks run without executing the code and are the cheapest gate:

  • Linters/formatters (ESLint, ktlint/detekt, Checkstyle, Black, gofmt): style and common bugs.
  • Type checkers (TypeScript, mypy).
  • SonarQube/SonarCloud: bugs, code smells, duplication, coverage on new code, summarised in a quality gate (pass/fail, e.g. "no new critical issues, new-code coverage ≥ 80%").
  • Dependency and license checks.

Gate on new code rather than the whole legacy codebase, so teams can improve gradually without being blocked by old debt.

Worked example. Quality gate: new code coverage ≥ 80%, no new blocker/critical issues, duplication ≤ 3%. A PR adds untested logic → the check fails and merge is blocked.

Industry examples. Sonar is widely used in enterprises; Google enforces readability and style through automated presubmit checks.

Everyday analogy. Spell-check before sending a document: cheap, instant, catches obvious slips.

Common interview traps.

  • Gates so strict that people disable them; start with realistic thresholds and ratchet.
  • Reporting but not blocking: a warning nobody must fix.

notes.title: Security scanning in the pipeline (DevSecOps)
notes.html:
"Shift left": find security problems early when they are cheap to fix. Types of scans:

Scan Finds Example tools When
SAST insecure code patterns in source CodeQL, Semgrep, SonarQube every PR
SCA / dependency known-vulnerable libraries (CVEs) Dependabot, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check every PR + scheduled
Secret scanning leaked keys in git history Gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning every push
Container scan CVEs in image layers Trivy, Grype build + scheduled
IaC scan misconfig in Terraform/K8s Checkov, tfsec, Kubescape every PR
DAST vulnerabilities in the running app OWASP ZAP against staging

Supply-chain hardening: lock dependency versions, generate an SBOM (CycloneDX/SPDX), sign artifacts (Sigstore/cosign), reach SLSA build levels (provenance showing how an artifact was built).

Worked example. Log4Shell: teams with an SBOM and SCA queried "which services include log4j-core < 2.15" in minutes; teams without one grepped repositories for days.

Industry examples. GitHub CodeQL and Dependabot are built in; Google created SLSA and Sigstore after supply-chain attacks (SolarWinds 2020, Codecov 2021).

Everyday analogy. Airport security uses different machines for bags, liquids and people; one scan type does not catch everything.

Common interview traps.

  • Tools that produce 3,000 findings nobody triages: tune severity, fix critical first, set SLAs.
  • Scanning only at build time: new CVEs appear after release, so re-scan deployed images.

notes.title: Flaky tests, test data and environments
notes.html:
A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Causes: timing (sleeps), shared state or order dependence, real network calls, unseeded randomness, time zones/clock, parallel runs sharing a DB.

Handling: reproduce (run 100 times), isolate state per test, use fakes or Testcontainers, control the clock, quarantine (move out of the blocking set, ticket with owner and deadline), track flake rate per test. Automatic retries are a stopgap; they hide real concurrency bugs.

Test data: per-test fresh data or transactions rolled back; ephemeral environments (a full temporary stack per PR, destroyed after merge) avoid shared-staging collisions.

Worked example. A test fails 1 in 30 because it asserts a time within 100 ms. A pipeline with 40 such tests fails ~75% of runs, and people begin ignoring red builds.

Industry examples. Google reports roughly 1.5% of test runs flaky; Meta and Atlassian built dedicated flaky-test detection and quarantine systems.

Everyday analogy. A bathroom scale that shows different weights each morning is worse than none: you stop trusting it.

Common interview traps.

  • Thread.sleep(2000) instead of waiting on a condition.
  • A shared staging database used by every PR.

notes.title: Release gates, approvals and compliance
notes.html:
Not every change deserves the same ceremony. Typical production gates: all required checks green, code review, passing smoke test in staging, change window rules, and manual approval for sensitive systems (payments). In regulated industries, the pipeline produces the audit evidence (who approved, what version, test results, scan reports), replacing manual spreadsheets.

Keep humans for judgement (is this risky?) and machines for repetition (did tests pass?). Separation of duties: the author cannot be the sole approver of their own production change.

Worked example. A fintech's pipeline requires two approvals for the payments service, one for others, and records the artifact digest, commit, approver and scan results automatically per deploy.

Industry examples. SOC 2 and PCI DSS audits at banks and payment companies accept pipeline logs plus protected branches as evidence.

Everyday analogy. A bank vault needing two keys held by different people.

Common interview traps.

  • Manual approvals for everything creates queues and rubber-stamping.
  • Hotfix path that bypasses all checks permanently; define a fast but still-gated emergency path.

notes.title: Contract testing for microservices
notes.html:
With many services, end-to-end tests are slow and brittle. Contract testing checks the agreement between a consumer (which calls an API) and a provider (which serves it) in isolation. In consumer-driven contracts (Pact), the consumer records the requests it makes and responses it expects; the provider's pipeline replays them to prove it still satisfies every consumer. A broker stores contracts, and can-i-deploy tells you if a version is safe to release.

Related tools: OpenAPI schema checks and breaking-change detection (oasdiff, Buf for protobuf) in CI.

Worked example. A provider renames a JSON field userId to user_id. Unit tests pass, but the contract check fails because the mobile app and the billing service still expect userId: caught before release.

Industry examples. Pact is used at Atlassian, Spotify and many banks; Google uses Buf-style breaking-change checks for protobuf APIs.

Everyday analogy. A signed purchase order between buyer and seller: each side can test that it honours the order without meeting the other.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing contract tests replace all integration tests (they cover interfaces, not whole behaviour).
  • Provider teams ignoring consumer contracts.

notes.title: Performance and load testing in the pipeline
notes.html:
Performance is a feature that regresses silently. Types: load (expected traffic), stress (beyond capacity to find the breaking point), soak (hours, finds leaks), spike (sudden surge). Tools: k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust.

Pipeline use: a short smoke load test on every merge to staging with thresholds (p95 < 300ms, errors < 1%); a full load test nightly or before big launches against a production-like environment; compare with a baseline and fail on regressions. Use realistic data and traffic mix, warm up caches, and watch the system (CPU, DB, queue depth), not only the client.

// k6
export const options = { vus: 50, duration: "2m",
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"], http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"] } };

Worked example. A new ORM query adds an N+1 pattern: p95 goes from 120 ms to 900 ms at 50 users. The nightly threshold fails and points to the offending commit range.

Industry examples. Netflix, Shopify and many retailers rehearse peak events with load tests (Black Friday); LinkedIn built a load-testing platform tied to its release process.

Everyday analogy. Stress-testing a bridge with trucks before opening it to traffic.

Common interview traps.

  • Load testing a tiny staging environment and extrapolating linearly.
  • Looking at average latency instead of p95/p99.

notes.title: Test environments: ephemeral and shared
notes.html:
A shared staging environment becomes a bottleneck and a source of flakiness (everyone's changes mix). Ephemeral (preview) environments create a full stack per PR (namespace, database seeded with test data, URL) and destroy it on merge or after a TTL. Tools: Argo CD ApplicationSets, Vercel/Netlify previews, Okteto, Garden, Tilt, Uffizzi.

Challenges: cost (use TTLs, scale to zero, shared infrastructure with per-PR schemas), seed data (anonymised snapshots, never raw production PII), and dependencies on other teams' services (use mocks, contract tests or shared "stable" versions).

Worked example. QA reviews a PR on pr-482.preview.acme.com before merge, instead of waiting for a free slot on staging; the environment auto-deletes after merge.

Industry examples. Vercel popularised per-PR previews for front ends; Shopify and Spotify run namespace-per-PR environments on Kubernetes.

Everyday analogy. A pop-up test kitchen per chef instead of one crowded shared kitchen.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying production data with real customer PII into test environments.
  • Previews that never get deleted and run up the bill.

notes.title: Dependency management and update automation
notes.html:
Most code in your service is third-party. Controls: lockfiles (package-lock.json, poetry.lock, Gradle dependency locking) for reproducible builds; pinned versions; automated update PRs with Dependabot or Renovate, each running your full CI so upgrades are tested; vulnerability alerts with a fix SLA (critical within days); an allow-list/mirror for registries; license checks.

Beware typosquatting (a malicious reqeusts package) and dependency confusion (a public package overriding an internal name): use scoped names and registry rules.

Worked example. Renovate opens a weekly grouped PR for minor/patch bumps (auto-merge if CI is green) and separate PRs for majors, keeping the codebase near current at low effort.

Industry examples. The 2021 ua-parser-js and 2022 colors / faker incidents and the log4j crisis pushed companies to automate updates and track SBOMs.

Everyday analogy. Regularly servicing the car in small steps rather than ignoring it for ten years and facing one huge repair.

Common interview traps.

  • Never updating dependencies, so the eventual upgrade is enormous.
  • Auto-merging without good tests.

notes.title: Supply chain security: SBOM, SLSA and signing
notes.html:
Attackers target the build and dependencies rather than your code. Defences:

  • SBOM (Software Bill of Materials, CycloneDX/SPDX): an inventory of every component in an artifact.
  • Signing artifacts and images (Sigstore/cosign, keyless via OIDC identity) and verifying signatures at deploy time (admission controllers such as Kyverno or Sigstore policy-controller).
  • Provenance (SLSA levels): attestations proving which source, builder and steps produced an artifact; higher levels need hermetic, tamper-resistant builds.
  • Pin actions and base images by digest, use reproducible builds where possible, protect the build system itself, and use two-person review for pipeline changes.
cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:abc...
cosign verify ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:abc... --certificate-identity-regexp 'github.com/acme/.*'

Industry examples. SolarWinds (2020, tampered build), Codecov (2021, modified uploader script) and xz-utils (2024, malicious maintainer) are the standard case studies; Google's SLSA and the OpenSSF Scorecard came from them.

Everyday analogy. Food traceability: a label showing the farm, the factory and the inspector's seal for every ingredient.

Common interview traps.

  • Signing images but never verifying them.
  • Trusting a dependency only because it is popular.

notes.title: Code review and CODEOWNERS
notes.html:
Review catches design and logic problems machines miss and spreads knowledge. Make it efficient: small PRs, a PR template (what/why/how to test), automation handling style so reviewers discuss substance, CODEOWNERS to request the right reviewers (security team for auth code, platform team for pipeline files), and a target response time (for example within one working day).

Review the pipeline files with extra care: a workflow change can run arbitrary code with access to secrets. Require owner approval for .github/workflows/**, Terraform, and deployment manifests.

Worked example. A one-line workflow change adds pull_request_target plus a checkout of the PR head, exposing secrets to forks. CODEOWNERS routes it to the security reviewer, who rejects it.

Industry examples. Google's readability and OWNERS files, GitHub CODEOWNERS and required-reviewer rules in most large organisations.

Everyday analogy. An editor reading a book before printing, with a legal specialist for the risky chapters.

Common interview traps.

  • Rubber-stamp approvals on huge PRs.
  • No extra scrutiny for CI/CD and infrastructure changes.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Use the test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a small number of E2E/smoke tests, plus contract tests between services. Add cheap static analysis and quality gates focused on new code. Shift security left with SAST, dependency, secret, container, IaC and DAST scans, and harden the supply chain with SBOMs, signing and provenance. Fight flaky tests by isolating state, controlling time and quarantining. Make release gates proportional to risk and have the pipeline capture audit evidence.

questions.promptHtml: What is the test pyramid and which tests run at which stage of the pipeline?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Test strategy shows engineering maturity.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests with real dependencies in the middle, and a few slow end-to-end tests at the top. Unit tests run on every commit, integration tests on every PR, and a small set of E2E or smoke tests after deploy to staging or production. Contract tests keep service interfaces compatible; load tests run on a schedule.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Lower layers are faster, cheaper and less brittle, so most coverage should live there. An inverted pyramid ("ice-cream cone") yields slow, flaky feedback. Coverage percentage is a floor, not a goal; mutation testing measures whether tests would actually catch bugs.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Running every E2E test on every PR.
  • Chasing 100% coverage with assertion-free tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a contract test? → Verifies a consumer's expectations of a provider's API (Pact).
  2. Where do load tests go? → Scheduled or pre-release, against a production-like environment.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior balances confidence and speed and uses contract tests for microservices.

questions.promptHtml: What is a quality gate and why apply it to "new code" instead of the whole codebase?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical adoption of quality tooling on legacy systems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A quality gate is a pass/fail rule, such as no new critical issues and at least 80% coverage on changed code, that blocks merging. Applying it to new code lets a team with a messy legacy codebase stop adding debt immediately without being blocked by thousands of old issues.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Tools: linters and formatters, type checkers, SonarQube. Gates must be enforced (required checks) not merely reported. Ratchet thresholds gradually. Avoid thresholds so strict that people disable the check.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Gate set on total coverage, which barely moves.
  • Warnings nobody is required to fix.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where else do quality checks run? → Pre-commit hooks locally and in CI.
  2. What about false positives? → Suppress with justification and review.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior treats gate design as change management.

questions.promptHtml: What are SAST, SCA and DAST, and where does each fit in a pipeline?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Security knowledge is expected for 3 YOE and above.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SAST analyses source code for insecure patterns (CodeQL, Semgrep) on every PR. SCA checks dependencies for known vulnerabilities (Dependabot, Snyk) on every PR and on a schedule. DAST attacks the running application (OWASP ZAP) against staging. Add secret scanning, container image scanning (Trivy) and IaC scanning (Checkov).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Shift left, since early fixes are cheaper. Rescan deployed images regularly because new CVEs appear later. Triage by severity and exploitability with agreed fix SLAs; unfiltered thousands of findings get ignored. Supply chain: SBOM, signed artifacts, provenance (SLSA).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Alert fatigue from untriaged findings.
  • Scanning only at build time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How did Log4Shell show the value of SBOMs? → Teams could query affected images in minutes.
  2. Which scans block the build? → Critical vulnerabilities and detected secrets; the rest warn.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs triage SLAs and supply-chain controls.

questions.promptHtml: How do you deal with flaky tests in CI?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Flakiness destroys trust in the pipeline.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Track and reproduce them (run many times), find the cause, and fix it: timing sleeps, shared state or ordering, real network calls, uncontrolled time or randomness. Quarantine confirmed flaky tests out of the blocking set with an owner and deadline so they do not block everyone, and measure flake rate over time. Retries are a stopgap, not a fix.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: If 40 tests each fail 1 time in 30, nearly three quarters of pipeline runs fail, and people start re-running instead of reading failures. Isolation techniques: per-test data, Testcontainers, fake clocks, wait-on-condition instead of fixed sleeps, hermetic tests. Ephemeral environments per PR avoid shared-staging collisions.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Auto-retry that hides concurrency bugs.
  • Deleting tests instead of fixing the root cause.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you find the flaky ones? → CI analytics of pass/fail on the same commit.
  2. Quarantine risk? → Becomes a graveyard unless owned and time-boxed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior builds detection, ownership and a policy, not heroics.

questions.promptHtml: How do you balance manual approvals with automation in a regulated environment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real companies have compliance requirements.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Automate everything repeatable (tests, scans, deployments) and keep humans for judgement. Use protected branches, mandatory reviews, separation of duties (author cannot be the only approver) and approval gates on production environments, while the pipeline records the evidence automatically: who approved, what artifact digest, which scans and tests passed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Auditors (SOC 2, PCI DSS) accept pipeline logs and branch protection as evidence, replacing spreadsheet sign-offs. Approvals should scale with risk: two approvers for payments, one for low-risk services. Provide an emergency path that is fast but still logged and reviewed afterwards.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Manual approval for everything, causing queues and rubber-stamping.
  • A permanent bypass for hotfixes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you prove what is in production? → Immutable digests, deploy records and provenance.
  2. Emergency changes? → Break-glass role with alerting and post-hoc review.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior aligns controls to risk and automates evidence collection.

questions.contextHtml: Your 30-engineer team's CI pipeline now fails about 35% of runs for reasons unrelated to the change. Engineers click "re-run" until it is green. Pipeline time is 28 minutes. Last month a real regression merged because its failure was assumed to be "just flaky".
questions.promptHtml: How do you restore trust in the pipeline?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add automatic retries of the whole pipeline three times.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tests fail most? Do they fail on the same commit when re-run? Shared database or environment? Resource limits on runners?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Identify the top 10 flakiest tests from CI history and quarantine them with owners so the blocking set is reliable.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Shared state or ordering; fixed sleeps and timing; real network dependencies; overloaded runners.
  4. How I'd verify: Re-run suspect tests in a loop, check failures by runner and time, correlate with shared resources.
  5. Root cause: Typically a handful of tests and a shared staging database cause most failures.
  6. Fix: Isolate data per test (Testcontainers or ephemeral DB), replace sleeps with condition waits, control clocks, mock external networks, shard to cut run time.
  7. Prevention: Flake-rate dashboard, a rule that any flaky test is quarantined within a day, and a merge queue so green means green.
  8. Trade-offs: Quarantine temporarily lowers coverage; I accept it with a deadline over eroding trust.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Management wants new features, not test work → show lost engineer-hours: 35% failure × 28 min × reruns × team size.
  • Is retry ever OK? → Targeted retry for known external flakiness with reporting, not blanket.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After quarantining 14 tests and isolating the DB, flake rate dropped under 2% and developers stopped re-running by reflex.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries only.
  • Hire: identifies, quarantines, isolates.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the cost, builds prevention and ownership.

questions.promptHtml: What is consumer-driven contract testing and why use it instead of end-to-end tests between services?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Microservices need a scalable way to catch breaking API changes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The consumer records the requests it makes and the responses it expects as a contract; the provider's pipeline replays those contracts to prove it still satisfies every consumer. A broker stores contracts and a can-i-deploy check gates releases. It is faster and less brittle than end-to-end tests and lets teams deploy independently.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Pact is the common tool; OpenAPI diff and Buf catch breaking schema changes. Contract tests verify interfaces, not full behaviour, so they complement rather than replace integration tests.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking contract tests replace all integration tests.
  • Provider teams ignoring consumer contracts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Example catch? → A renamed JSON field that unit tests did not notice.
  2. Who owns contracts? → Consumers write them, providers verify them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior wires can-i-deploy into the release gate.

questions.promptHtml: How do you include performance testing in a CI/CD pipeline?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Performance regressions are usually found too late.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A short smoke load test with thresholds (for example p95 under 300 ms, errors under 1%) on each merge to staging, and a full load, stress and soak test nightly or before big launches in a production-like environment, compared against a baseline. Use realistic data and traffic mix, warm caches, and watch system metrics such as CPU, DB and queue depth.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Types: load (expected traffic), stress (find the breaking point), soak (find leaks), spike (sudden surge). Tools: k6, Gatling, JMeter, Locust. Failing on regression points to the commit range.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Extrapolating linearly from a tiny staging environment.
  • Judging by averages instead of p95/p99.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you run it? → Staging that mirrors production sizing.
  2. How do you stop flaky perf tests? → Stable environment, repeated runs, tolerance bands.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior sets budgets and compares with baselines automatically.

questions.promptHtml: Why use ephemeral per-PR environments instead of one shared staging environment?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shared staging is a common bottleneck.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A shared staging mixes everyone's changes, queues testers and produces flakiness. An ephemeral environment gives each PR its own full stack and URL for review and testing and is destroyed on merge or after a TTL, so tests are isolated and parallel. Costs are controlled with TTLs and scale-to-zero.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Challenges: cost, seed data (anonymised, never raw production PII), and dependencies on other teams' services (mocks, contracts or shared stable versions). Tools: Argo CD ApplicationSets, Okteto, Garden, Vercel previews.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Copying production data with real PII into test environments.
  • Previews that never get deleted.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you cut cost? → Shared infrastructure with per-PR schemas, TTL, autoscale to zero.
  2. Test data? → Synthetic or anonymised snapshots.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior balances isolation with cost and data protection.

questions.promptHtml: How do you manage third-party dependencies safely and keep them up to date?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most of your code is third-party.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use lockfiles and pinned versions for reproducible builds, automate update PRs with Dependabot or Renovate so each runs the full CI, alert on vulnerabilities with a fix SLA, mirror registries, and watch for typosquatting and dependency confusion by using scoped names and registry rules.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Group minor and patch updates (auto-merge if green), separate PRs for majors. Never updating makes the eventual upgrade huge.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Never updating dependencies.
  • Auto-merging with weak tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is dependency confusion? → A public package overriding an internal one with the same name.
  2. How do you prioritise CVEs? → Severity, exploitability and exposure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior sets update cadence, SLAs and test confidence.

questions.promptHtml: What are an SBOM, artifact signing and SLSA provenance, and how do they defend the supply chain?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Supply-chain attacks are a top concern.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An SBOM lists every component in an artifact so you can instantly find where a vulnerable library is used. Signing (Sigstore/cosign) proves an artifact came from your pipeline and verification at deploy time rejects anything else. SLSA provenance attests how, where and from what source an artifact was built, with higher levels requiring tamper-resistant builds.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Pin base images and actions by digest, protect the build system, require two-person review for pipeline changes. SolarWinds, Codecov and xz-utils are the standard case studies.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Signing but never verifying.
  • Trusting a dependency just because it is popular.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you verify? → Admission controller in the cluster.
  2. Keyless signing? → OIDC identity tied to the CI workflow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior closes the loop with verification policy.

questions.contextHtml: A contributor opens a PR that modifies .github/workflows/ci.yml to use pull_request_target and check out the PR head so that PRs from forks get "faster previews". The diff is 6 lines and a teammate has approved it as "tiny".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you prevent this class of mistake?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Approves because the change is small and tests pass.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does this workflow have secrets or write tokens? Does it run any code from the PR?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not merge; if already merged, revert and rotate any secrets the workflow could access.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: pull_request_target runs in the base repo context with secrets while checking out untrusted code, letting a fork's code exfiltrate them.
  4. How I'd verify: Read the workflow permissions and the steps that execute PR code; check recent runs from forks.
  5. Root cause: Pipeline changes were reviewed like normal code without security scrutiny.
  6. Fix: Use pull_request (no secrets) for untrusted code, or split into an unprivileged build and a privileged step that does not execute PR code.
  7. Prevention: CODEOWNERS requiring the security/platform team for .github/workflows/**, least-privilege permissions, actions pinned by SHA, workflow linting (zizmor, actionlint).
  8. Trade-offs: More review friction on pipeline files; accepted since they run with secrets.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need previews for forks → build artifacts unprivileged and deploy from a trusted workflow that never runs fork code.
  • Already compromised? → Rotate secrets, audit runs, review recent deploys.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A similar misconfiguration in a public repo let a drive-by PR print a deploy token to logs; the team moved to OIDC and CODEOWNERS on workflows.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves on size.
  • Hire: spots the secrets exposure.
  • Strong hire: fixes the pattern and adds ownership and linting.
